target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting one large Claude skill into smaller sub-skills that call Python tools for search and validation, after CloudWatch and OpenSearch latency logs showed where time went
bullet_feedback.problem: 'AI workflow generation' does not say what kind of workflow; the reader only learns two bullets later that these are test-data workflows. 'Claude skill' / 'sub-skills' is product-specific jargon, and the term a screener or recruiter matches for this work (an LLM agent that calls tools) never appears.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: An LLM screener scoring for 'AI agents', 'tool calling' or 'LLM' sees a vendor feature name instead. A recruiter reads 'workflow generation' as generic AI and misses that it is a latency fix on an internal developer tool.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: that the workflows are test-data workflows, and what a 'Claude skill' is (an LLM agent's instruction-and-tool package)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the object before the method ('test-data workflow generation') and add the generic term once ('Claude agent skill' or 'LLM agent'). Put 'LLM tool calling / AI agents' in the AI/ML Skills line instead of the bullet.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
bullet_feedback.problem: It opens with a 'Because ...' clause, so the action verb 'precomputed' only arrives about 75 characters in. It is the one bullet on the page that does not start with a verb.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Skimmers and parsers that pull the first verb of each bullet see 'Because' and lose the action. The design decision (precompute plus cache, keyed on category) is the interesting part, and it is buried.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the verb and object, then give the constraint as the reason, e.g. 'Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows, because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL table had strict access limits'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt the legacy tool developers use to create test-data workflows as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation, and 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it
bullet_feedback.problem: 'the legacy tool developers use' can be misread as the noun phrase 'legacy tool developers'. The bullet is plainly internal developer tooling, but the matchable phrase 'developer tools' / 'internal tooling' never appears anywhere on the page.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: 'Developer tools' is one of the intended profile's four pillars and shows up in Robinhood and Ramp postings ('build developer tools', 'engineering tools'), yet a keyword pass finds no hit.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase as 'the legacy internal developer tool used to create test-data workflows'. The facts stay the same; the parse is unambiguous and the term becomes matchable.

bullet_feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a Python pipeline that renders AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on multi-camera images as Open3D overlays for a vision-language model, and tuned its prompts so it picks right more often
bullet_feedback.problem: 'picks right more often' is the outcome, but it is vague and casual: it does not say what 'right' means (the correct or feasible grasp?) or by how much. Every other bullet in the Experience section ends on a concrete result or a defined mechanism.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: An ML-infra screener or interviewer cannot tell whether this was measured, and next to well-quantified neighbors it reads as the weakest claim on the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'picks right' means (selects the successful grasp candidate?) and whether an accuracy change was measured
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'picks right more often' with the actual selection criterion. If a measured before/after exists, state it; if not, describe the outcome as the selection task the VLM performs, without implying a number.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products, and personally built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for one, Tortuga, a class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
bullet_feedback.problem: Two separate claims (founding the studio, and a caching layer) are joined with 'and'. The bolded '20,000+ visits' is product traffic, not a result of the Redis work, but it sits where a result would go.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader who skims the bold may credit the caching with the traffic, or may ask what the cache actually changed. Either way the engineering contribution has no visible effect.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: why the cache was added (load during the launch spike? query latency?) so the 20,000+ visits reads as the load it handled rather than a result
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Frame the traffic as the reason for the cache (e.g. 'built Redis caching in front of Prisma ORM queries so Tortuga could handle 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days'), but only if that was the actual motivation. Otherwise keep the two facts visibly separate.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo’s public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate
bullet_feedback.problem: 'space-topic research tool' does not say what the tool does (a document search? a summarizer?), and 'Amazon Leo' is a newly renamed program many recruiters won't recognize.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is minor. The keywords (AWS CDK, infrastructure as code, CI/CD, Fargate) all parse, but a non-engineer can't restate what was deployed.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the research tool does for the policy team, in a few words
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Swap 'space-topic research tool' for a short functional description. Leave the infrastructure clause as it is, because it is good.

page_feedback.problem: Skills omits screener-form terms the bullets already prove: Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon Bedrock (Skills says only 'Bedrock'), OpenSearch under AWS, event-driven / stream processing (Kinesis to Lambda), caching, vector search / vector database (ChromaDB, SentenceBERT), storage engines (B+ tree, LSM-tree), LLM tool calling / AI agents, LLM evaluation (LLM-as-judge), Open3D, React Flow, C++17. 'LLMs' and 'CI/CD' are not expanded ('large language models', 'continuous integration/continuous deployment'); the Lyft posting says 'Continuous integration and deployment' verbatim.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Exact-match ATS filters (Greenhouse/Lever keyword search, Workday skills extraction) count the Skills block heavily. Each missing term is a free match the candidate has already earned. 'storage engines' and 'developer tools' are corpus terms the page supports but never names.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Add only terms backed by the bullets above, and spell out each acronym once in Skills. For example, AWS line: 'S3, Redshift, Bedrock'. Practices line: 'storage engines (B+ tree, LSM-tree), caching, event-driven stream processing'. AI/ML line: 'large language models (LLMs), LLM tool calling / agents, vector search'. Don't put any of these into bullets.

page_feedback.problem: Several Skills entries have no supporting bullet: REST APIs, API Gateway, Docker, Node.js, SQLAlchemy, PyTorch, and POSIX (in the project header). 'API development' and 'REST APIs' are among the most frequent terms in the backend postings (Affirm: 'API development/documentation'; Stripe and Robinhood: services/APIs), yet no bullet shows an API being built.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A 2026 LLM screener checks each skill against the experience text and down-weights unsupported ones. A human interviewer will ask 'where did you build a REST API?' and find nothing on the page.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only Skills entries the candidate can defend. If any described system exposes an API (e.g. the Leo research tool behind API Gateway, or the Tortuga backend), clarify that in its bullet. Otherwise accept that these are secondary and consider dropping POSIX from the project header if nothing POSIX-specific was used.

page_feedback.problem: In the extracted text each role's lines run company, then date, then title, then location ('Amazon Web Services / Sep 2026 – Dec 2026 / Software Development Engineer Intern / Redmond, WA'), so the date sits between employer and title. The project header puts a pipe-delimited tech list inside the project name ('IEX Order Book & Matching Engine | C++17, STL, POSIX, Linux perf').
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Workday and Lever usually still pair these correctly, but some parsers attach the date line to the wrong field or store the whole tech string as the project title. This is a small risk, not a failure.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: The two-column header layout is fine. If the LaTeX template allows, emit the title before the date in the text layer. Optionally move the project's tech list to its own italic line, as the job titles already are.

page_feedback.problem: Section order puts the IEX matching-engine project, the page's strongest evidence of performance-sensitive systems (50.9M messages replayed, 1.26M events/sec, B+ tree vs LSM-tree), at the very bottom, below the single-bullet UMIACS role and the TerpLabs studio.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: For the stated 'systems-oriented engineer' profile, a 7-second skim catches AWS, Capital One and the Leo cloud work, but the performance/systems pillar is mostly seen only by readers who reach the last third of the page.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: This is a reorder only. Section headings stay standard either way. Consider whether UMIACS/TerpLabs or the IEX project better supports a backend application, and if it is the project, give it more vertical prominence (e.g. trim a TerpLabs line rather than an IEX one).

page_feedback.problem: Twelve of the thirteen bullets run to exactly two full lines, so the body is a uniform block of text with little whitespace between roles.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Bold metrics are sparse and do anchor the eye, but a uniform two-line rhythm makes every bullet look equally weighted, which slows the skim.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Where a bullet carries a setup clause ('Because ...', 'For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR,'), tighten it so a few bullets end early on the second line. Don't cut content just to make lines shorter.

page_feedback.problem: The employer line 'UMD App Development Contracting (Client: Amazon Leo)' puts a second Amazon entity in the employer field, next to the 'Amazon Web Services' internship.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Some parsers record the parenthetical as part of the employer name, which can show up as a duplicate or overlapping 'Amazon' employer in the ATS profile. A human reader understands it fine.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: This is acceptable as is. If parse previews show 'Amazon Leo' as an employer, move 'Client: Amazon Leo' into the title line or the first bullet.

keep: Writing Java logic that decides how much EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for operations like patching, setting upper and lower bounds that keep availability high without overspending, and backtesting the policies
Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda

Automated retraining for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance: on an EventBridge schedule a larger LLM grades its ratings, and fine-tuning runs only when the grades shift past a threshold

Building a RAG meal-suggestion feature for the official UMD app, in which GPT-4o mini writes suggestions from scraped recipes found by SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB, and internal testers rated 93% of meals satisfactory

Built a C++17 order book and matching engine and replayed 50.9M real IEX exchange messages through it without ever resyncing to the exchange’s book, matching 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices

Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads: the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range summaries for 27% more disk
Sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay, keeping each price level’s orders in a std::list FIFO inside a std::map and a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels
Standard section headings (Education, Experience, Projects, Technical Skills) and consistent 'Mon YYYY – Mon YYYY' date format throughout
Single-line contact header with email, LinkedIn and GitHub as plain text that extracts cleanly
AWS CDK (infrastructure as code) and GitHub Actions (CI/CD) written in both acronym and expanded form in Skills
